Tensor Analysis – Practical 8 Information: • Please make sure to complete all exercises before the next lecture. • The exercises marked with [See lecture] were solved in class. • The exercises are not organised by difficulty. 8.1 The Christoffel symbols of the first kind can be expressed in terms of the metric tensor as follows: Γijk = 1 2 ( ∂gik ∂xj + ∂gij ∂xk − ∂gkj ∂xi ) . This expression simplifies for orthogonal coordinate systems (those with gij = 0 when i ̸= j). Find the simplified expression for Γijk in the cases (1) i = j = k; (2) i = j ̸= k; (3) i ̸= j = k; (4) i, j, k are all distinct. 8.2 [See lecture] We have seen in Practical 5 spherical coordinates (x1, x2, x3) = (r, ϕ, θ), the metric tensors are g11 = 1, g22 = r2, g33 = r2 sin 2 ϕ, and the other components of the metric tensor are trivial. Find the Christoffel symbols of the first and second kind. 8.3 Consider the 2D coordinates (x1, x2) = (ρ, θ), in which the position vector r is given by r = ρ 2 cos(2θ) i1 + ρ 2 sin(2θ) i2, where i1, i2 are the usual 2-dimensional Cartesian basis vectors. (1) Find the corresponding basis vectors e1 and e2. (2) Find the covariant metric tensor gij and give your answer as a 2 × 2 matrix. Using the fact that the basis e1, e2 is orthogonal, find the contravariant metric tensor gij. (3) Find all Christoffel symbols Γijk of the first kind. (4) Find all Christoffel symbols Γi jk of the second kind. 1

2 8.4 Consider the coordinates (x1, x2, x3) = (x, y, t), in which the position vector r is given by r = (x2 − y2) i1 + (2xy) i2 + t i3, where i1, i2, i3 are the usual Cartesian basis vectors. (1) Find the corresponding basis vectors e1, e2, and e3. (2) Find the covariant metric tensor gij and the contravariant metric tensor gij. Give your final answer as 2 × 2 matrices. (3) Find all Christoffel symbols Γijk of the first kind. (4) Find all Christoffel symbols Γi jk of the second kind. 8.5 Given that the transformation law for the Christoffel symbol of the second kind is Γ i jk′ = L i′ ℓ L m j′ L n k′Γ ℓ mn + L i′ mL n k′ ∂Lm j′ ∂xn , show that the covariant derivative of a covariant vector is a second-rank covariant tensor. [Hint: You can use the equalities Lm k′ = ∂xm ∂x′k and Lr j′Lj′ ℓ = δr ·ℓ that we already have shown.]
